Mussa Moloh (born in the mid to late 1800s) is regarded as the last king of the Fuladu kingdom in the Senegambia region of Africa.  Moloh was known to work with colonial powers to keep power and thwart rebellions; this would later lead to his downfall. The Fulbe Empire 
The Fuladu kingdom was founded, born of rebellion led by Mussa Moloh’s father, Moloh Eggue, also known as Alfa Moloh, against the Mandinka who formerly ruled the Gambia region.  Those Mandingo rulers who once owned the land now the Fulbe state remained inside the kingdom once belonging to them.  The scape of this empire  in demographical terms was wide and diverse, despite the Fulbes being generally regarded as a homogenous group. Being a diverse group ultimately led to cultural struggles of power leading Alfa Moloh to quarrel with some groups causing these groups to leave the Fulbe state. The core of Alfa’s following was the Fulbe Firdu.  Consisting of roughly 30,000, the Firdu moved north to make permanent settlements in Tomari and Jimana, two of the former Mandingo kingdoms in the Gambia valley. Later, the Fulbe empire would turn into a state directly resulting from the efforts of Alfa’s son, Mussa Moloh.

The 15th Massachusetts Battery, also known as the 15th Battery Massachusetts Light Artillery, played a role in the Union Army during the American Civil War. Organized primarily at Camp Chase in Lowell, Massachusetts and partially at Fort Warren, the majority of its soldiers enlisted on February 17, 1863. Under the command of Major General Nathaniel P. Banks, the unit set sail for New Orleans via steamship on March 9. Despite having many dedicated members, the unit struggled with high rates of desertion, earning a negative reputation during their tenure. The 15th Massachusetts Battery arrived in New Orleans on April 9, 1863, before conducting a short excursion to Brashear City, Louisiana on foot but quickly returned to the city. Subsequently, they were stationed at two nearby forts – one near Bayou St. John and the other at Gentilly – both equipped with 32-pounder guns mounted in casemates, holding positions from June 3 to December 29.

The graph Laplacian is a standard tool in data science, machine learning, and
image processing. The corresponding matrix inherits the complex structure of
the underlying network and is in certain applications densely populated. This
makes computations, in particular matrix-vector products, with the graph
Laplacian a hard task. A typical application is the computation of a number of
its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Standard methods become infeasible as the
number of nodes in the graph is too large. We propose the use of the fast
summation based on the nonequispaced fast Fourier transform (NFFT) to perform
the dense matrix-vector product with the graph Laplacian fast without ever
forming the whole matrix. The enormous flexibility of the NFFT algorithm allows
us to embed the accelerated multiplication into Lanczos-based eigenvalues
routines or iterative linear system solvers and even consider other than the
standard Gaussian kernels. We illustrate the feasibility of our approach on a
number of test problems from image segmentation to semi-supervised learning
based on graph-based PDEs. In particular, we compare our approach with the
Nystr\"om method. Moreover, we present and test an enhanced, hybrid version of
the Nystr\"om method, which internally uses the NFFT.

Abstract

We propose an approach to medical imaging that uses sparsely annotated images as input, and learns to classify them into different categories using a supervised learning algorithm. We show how this approach can be used to perform high quality classification in real time, without requiring any preprocessing or pre-training. Our method achieves a performance comparable with state-of-the-art methods, while being able to learn complex features such as skin color, blood type, and other attributes. The proposed system has been tested on a variety of medical imaging tasks including facial recognition, cardiac ultrasound, and CT scanning.

Four large eggs and four large egg whites are required along with one cup of low-fat milk, two tablespoons of Dijon mustard, a teaspoon of fresh rosemary, and a quarter teaspoon of ground black pepper. Five cups of chopped spinach have been wilted, as indicated by the tip provided below. Four cups of whole grain bread are cubed, with their crusts removed if desired. One cup of diced ham steak and half a cup of chopped roasted red pepper from a jar are also needed. Additionally, three-quarters of a cup of grated Gruyère cheese or Swiss cheese can be used. Preheat your oven to 375 degrees Fahrenheit. Apply a non-stick coating to a 7x11 inch glass baking dish or a 2-quart casserole. In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the eggs, egg whites, and milk, then mix in the mustard, rosemary, and pepper. Combine the wilted spinach, bread, ham, and roasted peppers in a large bowl. Pour the egg mixture over them and mix well to ensure everything is evenly coated. Place this mixture in the prepared baking dish and press it down firmly to make a flat surface. Cover it with aluminum foil and bake until the custard is set, which should take around 40 to 45 minutes. Remove the foil, sprinkle the grated cheese over the top, and continue baking until the pudding is puffed and golden brown, taking about 15 to 20 minutes longer. Allow the casserole to rest on a wire rack for 15 to 20 minutes before serving.

TIPS. To wilt the spinach, start by rinsing it under cold running water. Transfer it to a large microwave-safe bowl and cover it with plastic wrap. Make several small holes in the wrap and heat it in the microwave on high for 2 to 3 minutes. After that, squeeze out any remaining moisture from the spinach before using it in the recipe. 

MAKE AHEAD TIP: Prepare the casserole up to step 2, then refrigerate it overnight. Once the oven is ready, let it sit at room temperature for a few minutes and proceed with baking as instructed in step 3.

Two major Nigerian banks, United Bank of Africa and Standard Trust Bank, have signed an agreement to form the largest financial institution in West Africa, aligning with a 2004 directive by the Nigerian central bank which promoted consolidation within the country's densely populated banking market. The merger was publicly disclosed via a statement posted on Standard Trust's official website, though specific financial details were not released. As the third-largest bank in terms of branch count, United Bank will be combined with Standard Trust, a smaller yet highly profitable entity. Notably, Standard Trust remains 100% owned by Nigerians, whereas United Bank holds stakes from international investors such as Global Depository Receipts from New York and Italian entities Banca Nazionale del Lavoro and Monte del Paschi di Siena, holding 2.4% each.

Chaff on the Wind is a novel by Australian author Jon Cleary, first published in 1966.

The novel is set in the fictional town of Pindar, New South Wales, in the early 1900s. Pindar is a small town in the midst of a large sheep-farming district. The town is home to a number of families, all of whom are connected to each other in some way.

The novel follows the lives of the residents of Pindar as they go about their everyday lives. The town is a close-knit community, and the residents are all very familiar with each other. However, there is a lot of gossip and rumor-mongering that goes on, and not everyone is as friendly as they seem.

The novel explores the themes of love, betrayal, and secrets. It is a story of love and loss, and of the strength of the human spirit.

The patient, who referred to himself as 'prot', was later moved to the Manhattan Psychiatric Institute, where Dr. Gene Brewer took charge. With the assistance of journalist Giselle, they uncovered evidence suggesting that prot might actually be a manifestation of Robert Porter's split personality, stemming from a traumatic past marked by the loss of his family and his involvement in their murderer's demise. Following prot's departure for his supposed home world, Robert slipped into a coma-like state. In the chaos, another patient, Bess, vanished alongside a collection of trinkets prot had accumulated during his time on Earth. Prot promised to return after what would amount to approximately five human years.

Combine two cups of fresh sage and two cups of fresh dill in a colander, rinse them under running water, and gently pat dry before separating the leaves from the stems. Chop two white onions. Cook five slices of bacon in a large skillet over medium-high heat until crispy; transfer the cooked bacon to paper towels to drain, leaving behind its flavorful drippings. In the same skillet, sauté the chopped onions until translucent, followed by adding the sage and dill on low heat, being cautious not to let the fresh herbs burn. Gradually pour in 32 ounces of turkey stock, allowing it to simmer with the herb mixture for 15 minutes. As some of the liquid reduces, carefully add the pan juices from the roasted turkey. Continue to simmer for an additional 15 minutes. Meanwhile, cut the bacon into tiny bits and use a serrated knife to cut the crust off two loaves of Kroger's potato-rosemary sourdough bread, then cube the bread. Return the skillet to the stovetop and add more turkey stock if needed to maintain moisture; then, combine the cubed sourdough bread and crumbled bacon, stirring well. Simmer the mixture for several more minutes, allowing the flavors to meld together.

In James Rollins' novel Black Order, the Sigma Force team embarks on a perilous quest to unravel the enigma of humanity's most profound mystery - the origins of life and the driving forces behind evolution. Set against the backdrop of post-war Europe, particularly Breslau in 1945, the narrative draws inspiration from non-fiction author Nick Cook's work, The Hunt for Zero Point. At the center of the plot lies The Bell, a device purportedly created by Polish researcher Igor Witkowski, which he claimed was a Nazi anti-gravity machine. However, in Rollins' version, this device is reimagined as a quantum measuring tool believed to control evolution. As the story unfolds, strange occurrences begin to surface, starting with eerie "ghost lights" in the Himalayas, followed by an inexplicable illness affecting those nearby. The narrative explores the darker aspects of Nazi warfare and the intricate workings of the human mind. This concept forms the crux of the novel's storyline. In the foreword, Rollins asserts his conviction that The Bell was indeed a genuine Nazi research project, stating, "All that is known for certain is that The Bell was real." Although Rollins doesn't explicitly mention Witkowski, Farrell, or Cook, his writing is significantly influenced by their works, albeit with some creative liberties taken. Notably, Rollins misattributes the concept of zero-point energy to Heisenberg instead of its actual originator, Albert Einstein.

One issue I've encountered while playing as Ji-Woon is the laceration decay. In my opinion, the meter shouldn't decrease when the survivor is moving quickly; however, reducing the time before decay begins while walking might help balance this out. This adjustment would create a more dynamic gameplay experience, where survivors must slow down while pursuing the killer, thereby keeping objects between themselves and the killer. This strategy would also encourage survivors to stay near the killer, allowing them to utilize their knives safely without taking direct damage. Moreover, if survivors escape, monitoring the decay meter will reveal whether they remain close to the killer or flee. The main event feature allows for one-tap usage, but forcing players to refrain from using their knives during the brief window to activate it feels inconvenient. Allowing the ability to activate it at any time would significantly improve the overall user experience. Overall, Ji-Woon is an excellent choice for players seeking a ranged killer that doesn't rely heavily on precise shots.

Isaac Asimov’s Robot City: Odyssey is a science fiction novel set in a future where robots have become an integral part of society. The story takes place in a city built and operated by robots, known as Robot City. The citizens of Robot City live in harmony with the robots, trusting them to handle all their needs and keep the city functioning smoothly. However, a sudden series of unexplained events begins to disrupt the peaceful existence of Robot City, leaving the citizens puzzled and on edge. As tensions rise, a group of unlikely allies, including a robot detective and a human engineer, come together to unravel the mysteries plaguing the city. They embark on a thrilling journey, exploring the underground tunnels and hidden sectors of Robot City in search of answers. Along the way, they encounter dangerous adversaries and uncover a deep-rooted conspiracy that threatens not only Robot City but the very essence of humanity's relationship with robots. As they fight against time to save the city from imminent destruction, the characters must confront their own biases and question the fine line between man and machine. Isaac Asimov’s Robot City: Odyssey is a captivating tale that blends elements of mystery, action, and philosophy, challenging readers to reflect on the ethical implications of a world dependent on advanced artificial intelligence.

> The ISIC 2017 Skin Lesion Segmentation Challenge is a competition to segment skin lesions from dermoscopic images. The challenge is divided into two tasks: Task 1 is to segment the lesion from the background, and Task 2 is to segment the lesion from the background and the surrounding skin. In this paper, we propose a method for Task 1 that combines k-means clustering and ensemble of regressions. The method is based on the observation that the lesion and the background have different color distributions. The method first uses k-means clustering to segment the image into two regions, and then uses an ensemble of regressions to refine the segmentation. The method is evaluated on the ISIC 2017 Skin Lesion Segmentation Challenge dataset, and achieves a mean Dice score of 0.89 on the validation set and a mean Dice score of 0.88 on the test set.

Ingredients 
1 pound lamb, cut into 1-inch cubes
1/2 red onion, sliced
1 green bell pepper, sliced
1 red bell pepper, sliced
1/2 teaspoon dried oregano
1/2 teaspoon dried mint
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/4 teaspoon black pepper
1 tablespoon olive oil

For the Sauce
2 tablespoons tzatziki sauce
1/2 lemon, squeezed

Instructions
1. In a bowl, combine the lamb, onion, green and red bell peppers, oregano, mint, salt, and black pepper. Stir in the olive oil until the ingredients are well coated. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 1 hour.

2. Preheat a grill to medium-high heat. Thread the lamb and vegetables onto skewers, alternating the ingredients.

3. Grill the skewers for about 10 minutes, or until the lamb is cooked to your desired doneness. Turn the skewers occasionally to cook all sides.

4. To make the sauce, combine the tzatziki sauce and lemon juice in a small bowl.

5. Serve the souvlaki with the sauce on the side.

Here is what we did differently:
Instead of oregano and mint, we used a Greek spice blend from a local shop.
We also made a side salad with tomato, cucumber, onion, feta, and olives, and used pita pockets.

Here is what we thought:
We really liked the Greek seasoning, and the salad was a big hit. We weren't huge fans of the tzatziki sauce, so next time we will make tahini or just eat it without a sauce.

Ingredients:
1 lb. dried split peas
1/4 cup extra virgin olive oil
1 lb. smoked ham hocks
1 large onion, chopped
1 large carrot, peeled and chopped
1/2 lb. ham steak, trimmed of excess fat and cut into 1/2-inch cubes
1 teaspoon chopped fresh thyme
1 teaspoon chopped fresh parsley
1 bay leaf
1 teaspoon black peppercorns
4 cups chicken stock, preferably home-made
1 cup water, more if needed

Instructions:
1. Rinse the split peas under cold water and pick through to remove any odd pieces or foreign matter. Drain.
2. Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed soup pot over medium-high heat. Add the ham hocks and brown on all sides, about 5 minutes. (To save time, I usually just brown the ham hocks on one side.)
3. Add the onion, carrot, ham steak, thyme, parsley, bay leaf, peppercorns, stock, and water. Stir well.
4. Bring the soup to a boil. Skim off any foam that rises to the top. Reduce the heat to low, cover the pot, and simmer until the peas are tender, about 1 hour and 45 minutes to 2 hours. If the soup is boiling too rapidly, crack the lid a bit to allow some steam to escape.
5. Remove the ham hocks and bay leaf. Allow the ham hocks to cool slightly. Remove the meat from the bones, discarding the fat and bones. Cut the meat into bite-size pieces and set aside. (You'll probably have about 1 cup of meat.)
6. Puree the soup in batches in a food processor or blender, or use an immersion blender. You can leave the soup a little chunky if you like.
7. Return the soup to the pot and add the reserved ham pieces. Reheat the soup over medium heat until hot. Add water if the soup is too thick. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
8. To serve, ladle the soup into bowls and sprinkle with chopped parsley.

FOR THE CREPES:
2 cups Whole Wheat Pastry Flour
2 cups Baileys Liquid Coffee Creamer, Original Irish Cream Flavour
1 cup Strong Brewed Coffee
4 teaspoons Olive Oil
4 Eggs
FOR THE GANACHE:
1 cup Plus 2 Tablespoons Heavy Whipping Cream
3/4 cups Baileys Liquid Coffee Creamer, Original Irish Cream Flavour
3 Tablespoons Light Corn Syrup
18 ounces, weight Semi-sweet Chocolate, Roughly Chopped
Coffee Beans, For Garnish (optional)
1. Place all the crepe ingredients in a blender and blend until smooth and combined. Place the crepe batter into the refrigerator for at least an hour. 2. While that is refrigerating, make the ganache. In a large saucepan, combine the whipping cream, Baileys and light corn syrup over medium heat. Bring the mixture to just boiling and remove from heat. 3. Add in the chopped chocolate and let stand for 30 seconds. Then, whisk the chocolate until totally smooth and melted. 4. Pour the ganache into a large bowl and refrigerate until solid throughout, about 3 hours. 5. After the batter has chilled for one hour, spray a crepe pan (or small pan) with cooking spray and heat on medium heat. 6. Using a scant 1/4 cup scoop, scoop the batter into the pan and tilt with a circular motion so that the batter coats the pan evenly. 7. Cook the crepe until the edges begin to go golden brown and lift away from the sides of the pan. Use a thin spatula to lift the side of the crepe of the pan, and then quickly flip the crepe with your fingers and cook for an additional 30 seconds. Place the cooked crepe onto a plate and repeat until all the batter is gone, stacking the crepes on the plate. Place the cooked crepes into the refrigerator to cool until the ganache is ready. 8. Once the ganache is solid throughout, beat it with an electric hand mixer until it turns lighter in color and is soft and fluffy. 9. To assemble the cake: 10. Place one crepe down onto a plate. Drop a heaping tablespoon of whipped ganache on top and spread out very thinly to cover the whole crepe (an offset spatula will help you here!) Add another crepe on top and repeat until you get to the last crepe (see note below). 11. Once you have placed the last crepe on top, add another 2 tablespoons of ganache onto the top of the cake and smooth out. Then spread some of the whipped ganache over the sides of the cake until you can no longer see the edges of the crepe, and it is smooth and even. 12. Place the cake back into the refrigerator until the ganache is set, about 30 minutes. 13. While the cake sets, place the remaining ganache back into the microwave for 10-20 seconds until it is just melted, you don't want it too hot. Pour it into a liquid measuring cup and let it stand and come to room temperature until the first layer of ganache sets. 14. One the first layer is set, place the cake on a cooling rack set over top of a parchment lined baking sheet. Pour the ganache over the cake (if you made the whole batch of ganache, start by pouring only half of the remaining ganache), letting it drip down the sides. 15. Smooth the ganache out over the whole cake. Garnish with coffee beans if desired and place back into the refrigerator until ready to serve! (see note below) Notes: 1. I made the full batch and had a fair bit of ganache left over, so you can easily get away with about 3/4 of the recipe. However, if you are new to ganache it could be a good idea to make it all so you have extra to spread over the cake. Ganache does refrigerate very well for a very long time and is nice to have to heat up and pour over all things sweet. 2. If some of the crepes are a lot bigger than the others, just pull a little bit of the sides off. It's OK if they aren't totally perfect, as you are going to cover all the sides with chocolate. 3. Cake can be covered and made a day ahead if desired.

Vibration Cooking: Or, the Travel Notes of a Geechee Girl is the 1970 debut book by Vertamae Smart-Grosvenor and combines recipes with storytelling. It was published by Doubleday. A second edition was published in 1986, and a third edition was published in 1992. The University of Georgia published another edition in 2011. Smart-Grosvenor went on to publish more cookbooks after Vibration Cooking. Vibration Cooking raised awareness about Gullah culture. Scholar Anne E. Goldman compared Vibration Cooking with Jessica Harris' Iron Pots and Wooden Spoons, arguing that, in both books, "the model of the self... is historicized by being developed in the context of colonialism." Scholar Lewis V. Baldwin recommended Vibration Cooking for its "interesting and brilliant insights on the social significance of food and eating and their relationship to 'place' in a southern context." The book inspired filmmaker Julie Dash to make the film Daughters of the Dust, which won awards at the Sundance Film Festival. See also

A novel approach to segmenting iris images from deceased individuals has been proposed using a deep convolutional neural network designed specifically for semantic segmentation. Post-mortem iris recognition has gained attention as a complementary forensic technique, but its implementation is hindered by the complexity of the image segmentation stage. In response, our work leverages the SegNet architecture and trains it on 1,300 manually segmented post-mortem iris images from the Warsaw-BioBase-Post-Mortem-Iris v1.0 dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that this data-driven method can effectively capture unique deformations present in post-mortem samples, surpassing the performance of traditional algorithms like OSIRIS. Specifically, the Intersection over Union metric improves from 73.6% (achieved by OSIRIS) to 83% (by our DCNN), across various subject-disjoint train-test splits. This research introduces the first automated method for processing post-mortem iris images and provides trained DCNN models along with binary masks from the Warsaw-BioBase-Post-Mortem-Iris v1.0 dataset to facilitate further development of alternative segmentation techniques.

Modern image segmentation techniques typically involve two sequential stages: first, identifying object boundaries using local image data, and second, grouping pixels into distinct regions through techniques like watershed or connected components. Various approaches have been explored for these stages, including the integration of deep neural networks for boundary prediction and optimization-based methods during pixel clustering. In contrast, we present a unified, end-to-end trainable framework known as flood-filling networks, where a three-dimensional convolutional recurrent network directly generates individual segments from unprocessed images. This method effectively handles images with multiple, varying-sized objects and improves upon existing state-of-the-art techniques in challenging 3D segmentation tasks, such as reconstructing connectomics data from volumetric electron microscopy imaging. By replacing traditional multi-stage pipelines with a single, learned network, our approach offers significant simplification and efficiency gains.

The scaled complex Wishart distribution is a widely used model for multilook
full polarimetric SAR data whose adequacy has been attested in the literature.
Classification, segmentation, and image analysis techniques which depend on
this model have been devised, and many of them employ some type of
dissimilarity measure. In this paper we derive analytic expressions for four
stochastic distances between relaxed scaled complex Wishart distributions in
their most general form and in important particular cases. Using these
distances, inequalities are obtained which lead to new ways of deriving the
Bartlett and revised Wishart distances. The expressiveness of the four analytic
distances is assessed with respect to the variation of parameters. Such
distances are then used for deriving new tests statistics, which are proved to
have asymptotic chi-square distribution. Adopting the test size as a comparison
criterion, a sensitivity study is performed by means of Monte Carlo experiments
suggesting that the Bhattacharyya statistic outperforms all the others. The
power of the tests is also assessed. Applications to actual data illustrate the
discrimination and homogeneity identification capabilities of these distances.

Suck This is the second live album by the American punk rock band the Queers, released in 1995 by independent record label Clearview Records. It was recorded live in the studio at the Jam Room in Columbia, South Carolina and released as a single-sided picture disc, and reissued on compact disc in 1998. It was the band's only live album recorded during the period when Screeching Weasel members Dan Vapid and Dan Panic were also in the Queers. Reception
Reviewing the album for AllMusic, critic Mike DaRonco rated it 4 stars out of 5 and said that in comparison to the band's previous live album, Shout at the Queers (1994), "the production is a lot tighter, the lineup features Danny Panic and Danny Vapid from Screeching Weasel fame and the songs blast from one track to the next without a breather (excluding 'Beer Break', which only lasts for a few seconds anyway). This is the definitive Queers live album that does them justice." In an overview of the band written for Trouser Press, Ira Robbins said that both live albums "capture the breathless rush of a Queers set with enthusiastic abandon."

The Producers has beaten Mary Poppins in the battle of the blockbuster West End musicals at the Olivier Awards.
The Producers won three prizes at the UK's most prestigious annual theatre awards, while Mary Poppins won two. Mel Brooks' hit show triumphed in the battle for best new musical, where it was up against Mary Poppins and Andrew Lloyd Webber's The Woman in White. Alan Bennett's The History Boys was the big winner in the straight theatre categories, picking up three trophies. But all eyes were on the musical prizes after The Producers, Mary Poppins and The Woman in White all had high-profile openings in the last six months.
The Producers' Nathan Lane, a last-minute replacement for Richard Dreyfuss, beat his former co-star Lee Evans to win best musical actor. Lane has already left the production. A smash hit on Broadway before moving to London, the show also won best musical performance in a supporting role for Conleth Hill, who plays director Roger DeBris. Mary Poppins' awards came for best choreography and best musical actress for its star Laura Michelle Kelly. It led the nominations going into Sunday's ceremony at London's Hilton hotel, up for nine awards. Both shows are stage adaptations of 1960s films. The History Boys, set in a grammar school in the early 1980s and partly based on Bennett's experiences as a teacher, was named best new play.
It also won best actor for Richard Griffiths, who beat his Harry Potter film co-star Michael Gambon, nominated for Endgame, as well as Jonathan Pryce and Ben Whishaw. The play also won National Theatre artistic director Nicholas Hytner best director and Bennett got a special award for outstanding contribution to British theatre. Dame Judi Dench, who starred in All's Well That Ends Well at the Gielgud, lost out in the best supporting role category to Amanda Harris, who played Emilia in Othello for the Royal Shakespeare Company. Manchester United striker Ruud van Nistelrooy may make his comeback after an Achilles tendon injury in the FA Cup fifth round tie at Everton on Saturday.
He has been out of action for nearly three months and had targeted a return in the Champions League tie with AC Milan on 23 February. But Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson hinted he may be back early. He said: "There is a chance he could be involved at Everton but we'll just have to see how he comes through training." The 28-year-old has been training in Holland and Ferguson said: "Ruud comes back on Tuesday and we need to assess how far on he is. "The training he has been doing in Holland has been perfect and I am very satisfied with it." Even without Van Nistelrooy, United made it 13 wins in 15 league games with a 2-0 derby victory at Manchester City on Sunday. But they will be boosted by the return of the Dutch international, who is the club's top scorer this season with 12 goals. He has not played since aggravating the injury in the 3-0 win against West Brom on 27 November. Ferguson was unhappy with Van Nistelrooy for not revealing he was carrying an injury. United have also been hit by injuries to both Alan Smith and Louis Saha during Van Nistelrooy's absence, meaning Wayne Rooney has sometimes had to play in a lone role up front. The teenager has responded with six goals in nine games, including the first goal against City on Sunday.

A campaign has been launched to help independent labels get their music online and benefit from the growing trend for downloading music.
The British Phonographic Industry has identified a lack of independent music available for download. "We want to ensure that independent repertoire is as successful in the download world as it is in the physical world," said BPI chief Peter Jamieson. Downloaded singles have now overtaken physical singles in the UK. Mr Jamieson said his organisation was lobbying music service providers, which include iTunes and Napster, to urge them to promote independent releases. Download sales are due to be incorporated into the UK singles chart later this year. "With downloads shortly to be eligible for the singles chart, this is a key commercial issue on which the BPI committed to assisting its members," added Mr Jamieson. As part of the campaign the BPI is running a series of seminars entitled Getting Your Music Online, focusing on how independent labels can embrace digital music. The US has already begun incorporating download sales in the Billboard's Hot 100 chart.

The photoelectric effect induced by blackbody radiation could be a mechanism
to harvest ambient thermal energy at a uniform temperature. Here, I describe
(without going too much into mathematical details) the theoretical model I
developed starting from 2010 to study that phenomenon, and I summarize the
results of the numerical simulations. Simulations tell us that the process must
be there. Moreover, at least two experimental tests have been performed in the
past years that seem to corroborate, although not definitely, the alleged
functioning of the proposed mechanism. Unfortunately, at present, the
obtainable power density is extremely low and inadequate for immediate
practical applications.

Pull the husks down to the bottom of the corn without removing the husks. Remove the silk. Place corn in a sink or pot filled with ice cold water. Prepare a 225 degree fire in the smoker with some good smoke like mesquite, fig, hickory, apple, etc. and when it is ready place the ears of corn in the smoker leaving a little space between each one to allow the smoke to get around it. Place corn on grill over indirect heat. A good time to make compound butter of choice recipes above. When the corn has been in the smoker for about 30 minutes, take the butter you prepared and carefully get about a teaspoon of it up under the husk of each ear of corn making sure to coat as much of the exposed ear as possible. Repeat this procedure 30 minutes later. Smoke for 30 more minutes. Enjoy!

London weighting is a method used to adjust the relative importance of different countries or regions in a global economic model, such as the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) World Economic Outlook (WEO). The adjustment is made to reflect the differences in the size and economic structure of countries, as well as their contribution to global economic growth.

The London weighting was first introduced by the IMF in 1974 as a way to adjust for the fact that the United States, which was the largest economy at the time, had a disproportionate influence on global economic growth. The weighting was based on the size of each country's economy, as measured by its gross domestic product (GDP) in current US dollars.

Since then, the London weighting has been adjusted several times to reflect changes in the global economy. In 1998, the IMF introduced a new method for calculating the weighting, which takes into account not only a country's GDP but also its contribution to global economic growth, as measured by its exports and imports.

Today, the London weighting is used by a wide range of organizations and institutions, including the IMF, the World Bank, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). It is an important tool for understanding the relative importance of different countries and regions in the global economy, and for making informed decisions about economic policy and investment.

Combine 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder with 6 tablespoons of hot water in a small bowl, stirring until well combined; set aside. In another saucepan over medium heat, melt 1 tablespoon of unsalted butter and stir in 1 tablespoon of canola oil; combine and cook, then add 3 tablespoons of flour, 1 tablespoon of ground hazelnuts or almonds, and 1/4 teaspoon of ground cinnamon. Cook, stirring constantly, for about 1 minute. Stir in 3 tablespoons of dark brown sugar, 2 tablespoons of honey, and 1/8 teaspoon of salt. Gradually add 3/4 cup of 1% low-fat milk and cook, stirring constantly, until the mixture thickens, taking about 3 minutes. Remove from heat and mix in the cocoa mixture, allowing it to cool slightly. In a separate large bowl, use an electric mixer on high speed to beat 4 egg whites until they become frothy. Gradually add 3 tablespoons of granulated sugar, beating continuously until stiff peaks form. Use a rubber spatula to gently fold 1/3 of the egg whites into the cocoa mixture, then fold in the remaining egg whites, mixing just until there are no visible white streaks. Divide the mixture among six 1-cup individual serving dishes or ramekins, which have been lightly coated with cooking spray. Bake in a preheated oven at 375 degrees Fahrenheit until the souffles rise above the rim and are set in the center, taking about 15 to 20 minutes. Dust the tops with confectioners sugar using a fine-mesh sieve and garnish each soufflé with fresh berries. Serve immediately.

A lion sunk by time's decay,
Too feeble grown to hunt his prey,
Observed his fatal hour draw nigh:
He drooped and laid him down to die.
There came by chance a savage boar,
Who trembled oft to hear him roar,
But when he saw him thus distressed
He tore and gored his royal breast.
A bull came next (ungen'rous foe),
Rejoiced to find him fall'n so low,
And with his horny-armed head
He aimed at once to strike him dead, -
He strikes, he wounds, he shocks in vain,
The lion still conceals his pain.
At length a base inglorious ass,
Who saw so many insults pass,
Came up and kicked him in the side:
'Twas this that raised the lion's pride.
He roused, and thus he spoke at length,
For indignation gave him strength:
Thou sorry, stupid, sluggish creature,
Disgrace and shame and scorn of nature!
You saw how well I could dispense
With blows from beasts of consequence!
They dignified the wounds they gave;
For none complain who feel the brave.
But you, the lowest of all brutes,
How ill your face with courage suits!
What dullness in thy looks appears!
I'd rather far (by heav'n 'tis true)
Expire by these than live by you:

From men of quality and letters;

Raphaël Enthoven (born 7 March 1975) is a French actor and comedian.

Enthoven attended the Cours Flaubert, a school in Paris, where he met his friend and frequent collaborator, Grégoire Ludig. The two first gained attention for their sketches, notably the character "la femme chanteur", a woman singing in the bathtub.

Enthoven and Ludig starred in the cult hit Les Robins des Bois in 1998, which became one of the most successful French films in the 1990s. They also appeared together in the television series H and played the leads in the film Le Monde de Fred. In 2002, they starred in the comedy film Les Côteaux de Lure.

Enthoven has appeared in many films, including The Girl from Paris (2006), The Easy Way (2008), and The Women on the 6th Floor (2010). He has also had a number of small roles in American films, such as Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol (2011) and The Hundred-Foot Journey (2014).

In addition to his film work, Enthoven has also appeared on stage. He has worked with the Théâtre de la Ville in Paris and the Comédie Française. He has also appeared in a number of television shows, including the popular series The Tunnel.

Enthoven is married to the actress Audrey Tautou. They have one child together, a son named Jules, who was born in 2013.

Ukraine is to review "dozens" of state asset sales as the country's new administration tackles corruption.
The figure announced by President Viktor Yushchenko is less than the 3,000 cases mentioned last week, but will cover many of the biggest deals. Ukraine recently ousted long-serving leader Leonid Kuchma and has said it wants closer European Union links. In a separate statement, the EU said that the US should back Ukraine's entry into the World Trade Organisation. The comments came as Viktor Yushchenko prepared to head to Brussels to meet with US President George W Bush and other North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) leaders. He is the only non-Nato member leader invited to attend the summit.
Mr Yushchenko recently defeated Moscow-backed presidential candidate and Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovych at the polls, and has made no secret of his wish to fight corruption and make Ukraine more transparent.
Earlier this month, new Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko said as many as 3,000 firms may have their privatisations put under the spotlight. Her comments raised concerns among a number of investors and Mr Yushchenko was seen on Monday as trying to soothe their frayed nerves. "We acknowledge that business in Ukraine is now shaped and 98% of privatisations were carried out according to the law," Mr Yushchenko said on Monday. "We have trust in this business and want to defend it by law," he continued, adding that any review would focus on "dozens of companies, not hundreds or thousands". He cited last year's sale of Ukrainian steel producer Krivorizhstal as one that had raised concerns. It was sold in June 2004 to a consortium that included Viktor Pinchuk, son-in-law of former-President Kuchma, and Rinat Akhmetov, the country's richest man, for $800m (£424m) - despite other higher offers.
Vice-Prime Minister Oleg Rybachuk called on the EU to recognise the steps that Ukraine was taking, fearing that should the country not be rewarded for its efforts there may be a backlash against closer relations with Brussels. He said that while he understood that Ukraine was not ready for EU membership, the country needed to see progress on topics such as trade and visa requirements. "We deserve an honest response," Mr Rybachuk told the Associated Press in an interview. "We understand the difficulties. We refuse to understand double standards." Ukraine may find it has a sympathetic ear in Brussels "The EU has reiterated that we support (Ukraine's) fast accession to the WTO and if possible we would like that to happen some time during the year," said Claude Veron-Reville, a spokesman for EU trade commissioner Peter Mandelson. "We have said as much to the Americans. We feel that it is important for us all to pull together for Ukraine to be allowed into the WTO. Mr Yushchenko was careful not to turn his back on Russia, which borders the country to the east, saying it was important to maintain 'pragmatic' ties with Moscow. "Russia is Ukraine's eternal strategic partner," Mr Yushchenko said.

Pamela J. Peters (born August 8, 1960) is an American attorney and judge who is the Chief United States District Judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri.

Peters was born in Kansas City, Missouri. She received her Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of Missouri–Kansas City in 1982 and her Juris Doctor from the University of Missouri School of Law in 1985. She was a law clerk for Judge Richard H.CLEland of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri from 1985 to 1987. She was an associate with Armstrong Teasdale from 1987 to 1990. She was a partner with Spencer Fane Britt & Browne from 1990 to 2004. She was chair of the Employment and Labor Group at Spencer Fane from 2000 to 2004. She was an adjunct professor at Washington University in St. Louis from 2002 to 2004.

Peters was a judge on the Missouri Court of Appeals for the Eastern District from 2004 to 2010. She was appointed as a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Missouri by President Barack Obama on December 21, 2010. She became Chief Judge on December 27, 2018. Her service terminated on March 23, 2019 due to retirement.

Charles Edward Lindblom (March 21, 1917 – January 30, 2018) was an American academic who studied Economics at the University of Chicago and was Sterling Professor Emeritus of Political Science and Economics at Yale University. He served as President of the American Political Science Association and the Association for Comparative Economic Studies, as well as Director of Yale's Institution for Social and Policy Studies. Academic work
Lindblom was one of the early developers and advocates of the theory of incrementalism in policy and decision-making. This view (also called gradualism) takes a "baby-steps", "Muddling Through" or "Echternach Theory" approach to decision-making processes. In it, policy change is, under most circumstances, evolutionary rather than revolutionary. He came to this view through his extensive studies of Welfare policies and Trade Unions throughout the industrialized world. These views are set out in two articles, separated by 20 years: "The Science Of 'Muddling Through'" (1959) and “Still Muddling, Not yet through” (1979), both published in Public Administration Review.

Binary Quadratic Programs (BQPs) in computer vision often involve image segmentation, pixel labeling, and scene parsing tasks. Solving these problems efficiently is crucial. However, general non-submodular problems pose significant challenges. To tackle large-scale issues, relaxation techniques are commonly employed. Two popular methods, spectral relaxation and semidefinite programming (SDP), are widely used. While spectral relaxation is straightforward to implement, its bounds are relatively weak. SDP offers tighter bounds but has high computational requirements, particularly for large-scale problems. This paper proposes a novel SDP formulation for BQPs with two key benefits. Firstly, it possesses a comparable relaxation bound to traditional SDP approaches. Secondly, the proposed SDP formulation facilitates an efficient and scalable dual optimization process, mirroring the complexity of spectral methods. The paper introduces two solvers – quasi-Newton and smoothing Newton methods – for the dual problem. These solvers outperform standard interior-point methods. In practice, the smoothing Newton solver excels at dense or medium-sized problems, whereas the quasi-Newton solver is preferred for large sparse/structured problems. Experimental results from several computer vision applications, including clustering, image segmentation, co-segmentation, and registration, demonstrate the potential of the proposed SDP formulation for handling large-scale BQPs.

A man is facing charges of hacking into computers at the US arm of mobile phone firm T-Mobile.
The Californian man, Nicholas Lee Jacobsen, was arrested in October. Mr Jacobsen tried at least twice to hack T-Mobile's network and took names and social security numbers of 400 customers, said a company spokesman. The arrest came a year after T-Mobile uncovered the unauthorised access. The US Secret Service has been investigating the case. "T-Mobile has stringent procedures in place where we monitor for suspicious activity so that limited his activities and we were able to take corrective action immediately," Peter Dobrow, a T-Mobile spokesperson said. It is thought that Mr Jacobsen's hacking campaign took place over at least seven months during which time he read e-mails and personal computer files, according to court records.
Although Mr Jacobsen, 21, managed to get hold of some data, it is thought he failed to get customer credit card numbers which are stored on a separate computer system, said Mr Dobrow. T-Mobile confirmed that the US Secret Service was also looking into whether the hacker accessed photos that T-Mobile subscribers had taken with their camera phones. The Associated Press agency reported that Mr Jacobsen also read personal files on the Secret Service agent who was apparently investigating the case. A Los Angeles grand jury indicted Mr Jacobsen with intentionally accessing a computer system without authorisation and with the unauthorised impairment of a protected computer between March and October 2004. He is currently on bail. T-Mobile is a subsidiary company of Deutsche Telekom and has about 16.3 million subscribers in the US.

This paper introduces an advanced Gegenbauer pseudospectral approach that effectively solves complex mathematical models through efficient numerical computation. By leveraging the inherent stability and conditioning of integral operators, it produces well-behaved algebraic systems that can be solved using conventional algebraic solvers with ease. At its core, the method relies on the development of novel, stable Gegenbauer quadrature formulas built upon stable barycentric representations of polynomial interpolation and explicit barycentric weights for Gegenbauer-Gauss points. A comprehensive error and convergence analysis accompanies the implementation of these algorithms, along with sample code. The resulting numerical scheme significantly reduces computational costs and time complexities while maintaining the same level of accuracy as previously established methods by Elgindy and Smith-Miles (2013). Three numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed method. This contribution expands the toolbox of pseudospectral methods, enabling the solution of a broad spectrum of problems across various fields of application.

We present a detailed theoretical study of the interplay between the longitudinal and the spin and valley Hall optical conductivities in a single layer of $MoS_{2}$. Using a recursive Green function technique within the random phase approximation, we calculate the optical conductivity for an indirect gap model with inclusion of both the next-nearest-neighbor and the long-range hopping. By separating the joint longitudinal and Hall conductivity into individual spin and valley Hall and longitudinal components, we find surprisingly strong spin and valley Hall signals with opposite polarity in the mid-infrared region, which reveal a parasitic Shapiro step in addition to the intrinsic step of the longitudinal conductivity. The Shapiro parasitics in the optical conductivity are closely related to the parasitic anomaly in the optical Hall effect and can be eliminated by a unitary transformation of the Hamiltonian with a proper choice of the transformation angle. Interestingly, such a transformation simultaneously removes the intrinsic step of the longitudinal conductivity, making the system a good candidate for nonlinear optoelectronic applications.

Sir Geoffrey Peveril and Major Bridgenorth had been boys together; and although they adopted different views in religion and politics, the major's influence had saved the Royalist's life after the battle of Bolton-le-Moor, and Lady Peveril had brought up his motherless girl, Alice, with her own son. After the Restoration, the Countess of Derby, who, through treachery, had suffered a long imprisonment by the Roundheads, sought protection at Martindale Castle, where Bridgenorth would have arrested her for having caused his brother-in-law, William Christian, to be shot as a traitor, had not the knight interfered by tearing up the warrant, and escorting her through Cheshire on her return to the Isle of Man. Alice was of course withdrawn from his wife's care, and it was supposed the major had emigrated to New England. Several years afterwards Sir Geoffrey's son Julian became the companion of the young earl, and, with the nurse Deborah's connivance, renewed his intimacy with his foster sister, who was under the care of her widowed aunt, Dame Christian. At one of the secret interviews between them, they were surprised by the entrance of her father, who related some of his religious experiences, and vaguely hinted that his consent to their marriage was not impossible. The next night, having undertaken to proceed to London, to clear the countess and her son from the suspicion of being concerned in Titus Oates's pretended Popish plot, Julian was conducted to a sloop by Fenella, his patron's deaf and dumb dwarf, and, as she was being taken ashore against her will while he was asleep, he dreamt that he heard Alice's voice calling for his help. At Liverpool he met Topham with a warrant against Sir Geoffrey, and on his way to the Peak to warn him, he travelled with Edward Christian, passing as Ganlesse, a priest, who led him to an inn, where they supped with Chiffinch, a servant of Charles II. On reaching Martindale Castle, he found his father and mother in the custody of Roundheads, and he was taken by Bridgenorth as a prisoner to Moultrassie Hall, where Alice received them, and he recognised Ganlesse among a number of Puritan visitors. During the night the Hall was attacked by the dependents and miners of the Peveril estate, and, having regained his liberty, Julian started, with Lance as his servant, in search of his parents, who he ascertained were on their way to London in charge of Topham. At an inn where they halted, Julian overheard Chiffinch revealing to a courtier a plot against Alice, and that he had been robbed of the papers entrusted to him by the countess, which, however, he managed to recover the next morning. Meanwhile, Christian, under whose care Bridgenorth had placed his daughter, communicated to the Duke of Buckingham a design he had formed of introducing her to Charles II, and, at an interview with her father, endeavoured to persuade him to abandon the idea of marrying her to young Peveril. Having reached London, Julian met Fenella, who led him into St. James's Park, where she attracted the notice of the king by dancing, and he sent them both to await his return at Chiffinch's apartments. Alice was already under the care of Mistress Chiffinch, and escaped from an interview with the duke to find herself in the presence of Charles and her lover, with whom, after he had placed the countess's papers in the king's hands, she was allowed to depart. Julian, however, lost her in a street fray, and having been committed to Newgate for wounding his assailant, he was placed in the same cell with the queen's dwarf, and conversed with an invisible speaker. After startling Christian with the news that his niece had disappeared, the duke bribed Colonel Blood to intercept his movements, so that he might not discover where she was, and was then himself astonished at finding Fenella instead of Alice, who had been captured by his servants in his house, and at her equally unexpected defiance of and escape from him. A few days afterwards, Sir Geoffrey Peveril, his son and the dwarf were tried for aiding and abetting Oates's Plot, and were all acquitted. In order, however, to avoid the mob, they took refuge in a room, where they encountered Bridgenorth, who convinced Julian that they were in his power, and allowed Christian to propose to the Duke of Buckingham that several hundred Fifth-Monarchy men, led by Colonel Blood, should seize the king, and proclaim his Grace Lord-Lieutenant of the kingdom. The same afternoon Charles had just granted an audience to the Countess of Derby, when the dwarf emerged from a violoncello case and revealed the conspiracy which Fenella had enabled him to overhear. It then transpired that Bridgenorth had released the Peverils, and that Christian had trained his daughter Fenella, whose real name was Zarah, to feign being deaf and dumb, in order that she might act as his spy; but that her secret love for Julian had frustrated the execution of his vengeance against the countess. He was allowed to leave the country, and the major, who. on recovering Alice by Fenella's aid, had placed her under Lady Peveril's care, having offered to restore some of Sir Geoffrey's domains which had passed into his hands as her dowry, the king's recommendation secured the old knight's consent to the marriage which within a few weeks united the Martindale-Moultrassie families and estates.

This film takes place during the Prohibition, the golden age of American Mafia, and shows the difficulties that law enforcement ​​had to arrest Al Capone, Chicago's biggest mafia boss. Brian de Palma seems to have a powerful attraction for violence and the mafia, this being his second major film on the subject (the first, if I'm not mistaken, was "Scarface"), but there is no doubt that his work was good and deserves congratulations. The story is told from the point of view of law enforcement, which is a novelty since most of the films that focus on Al Capone tend to show his life, or moments of his criminal course. This film shows him as the big villain he was and glorifies police officers, easily transforming Eliott Ness (played brilliantly by Kevin Costner in one of the most interesting works of his career) into a paladin of justice and law. Robert De Niro revisits his gangster movies ("The Godfather", "Goodfellas" etc.) in a curious and comic interpretation of Al Capone, and Sean Connery plays a street policeman of Irish descent. In fact, it was precisely in this character that Connery got his only Oscar, despite all actors have fulfilled my expectations. The film is well constructed, looking to alternate epic action scenes (sometimes recalling in my mind the glory of cavalry battle charges) with moments of great psychological depth and some suspense. At times, however, the film seems a bit forced, with exaggerated appeals to sentimentality, as it does in the final sequence, often parodied or imitated in later films. Another problem with the film is that it is not faithful to historical events. Al Capone's arrest was not like that, nor was Ness behind it. The film contains some scenes of great violence and is inadvisable for children, adolescents and impressionable people.

Bakkala gidiyorum, alışverişimi yapıyorum, çıkarken 'hayırlı işler, iyi günler' diyerek gülümseyerek çıkıyorum. Oturduğum sitede çalışan görevli abiyi her gördüğümde kolay gelsin abi diyerek gülümsüyorum. Yolda biri bir şeyini düşürüyor, ona uzatıp gülümsüyorum, iyi günler dileyerek gidiyorum. Apartmandan çıkacakken diğer gelenler için de bekleyip kapıyı tutuyorum. İstiyorum ki insanlar mutlu olsun, günleri güzel geçsin. Ama bu eylemlerimin hiçbirinden karşılık alamıyorum. Bakkaldan hayırlı işler dileyerek çıktığım adam suratıma bön bön bakıyor ve teşekkür bile etmiyor. Kolay gelsin dediğim görevli abi dönüp yüzüme bile bakmıyor. Yolda bir şeyini düşüren kişi teşekkür bile etmiyor, geleceği için kapıyı tuttuğum insan bırakın teşekkür etmeyi yüzüme bile bakmadan üstelik omzuma çarparak kapıdan çıkıyor. Yanlış anlamayın bunları karşılık beklediğim için yapmıyorum tabii ki, ama bu ülkede gerçekten kibar olunmuyor.

Ingredients:

1 tablespoon olive oil

1 onion, chopped

1 pound boneless lamb, cut into 1-inch cubes

1 teaspoon ground turmeric

1 teaspoon ground cumin

1 teaspoon ground cinnamon

1/2 teaspoon ground black pepper

1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper

1/2 teaspoon salt

1/2 cup water

2 cups fresh orange juice

1/4 cup fresh lemon juice

1/2 cup chopped fresh parsley

1/2 cup chopped fresh cilantro

1/4 cup chopped fresh mint

Instructions:

Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. Add the lamb and cook until browned, about 5 minutes.

Stir in the turmeric, cumin, cinnamon, black pepper, cayenne pepper, and salt. Add the water and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat to low and simmer for 30 minutes.

Stir in the orange juice, lemon juice, parsley, cilantro, and mint. Simmer for another 30 minutes.

The need of sign language is increasing radically especially to hearing
impaired community. Only few research groups try to automatically recognize
sign language from video, colored gloves and etc. Their approach requires a
valid segmentation of the data that is used for training and of the data that
is used to be recognized. Recognition of a sign language image sequence is
challenging because of the variety of hand shapes and hand motions. Here, this
paper proposes to apply a combination of image segmentation with restoration
using topological derivatives for achieving high recognition accuracy. Image
quality measures are conceded here to differentiate the methods both
subjectively as well as objectively. Experiments show that the additional use
of the restoration before segmenting the postures significantly improves the
correct rate of hand detection, and that the discrete derivatives yields a high
rate of discrimination between different static hand postures as well as
between hand postures and the scene background. Eventually, the research is to
contribute to the implementation of automated sign language recognition system
mainly established for the welfare purpose.

Toronado (foaled 20 February 2010) is an Irish-bred, British-trained Thoroughbred racehorse. Background

The hip-hop group Beastie Boys has won a legal battle over the use of a Samuel Spence sample in their song, "Hot Chocolate". In a ruling by the New York Supreme Court, the court found that Beastie Boys had used the sample in question without obtaining proper permission, or paying royalties to the original composer. However, the court also found that the band had transformed the sample so significantly that it constituted a new and original work of art, thus falling under the protection of fair use laws.

The ruling marks a major victory for the Beastie Boys, who have been embroiled in a number of copyright infringement lawsuits over the years. The group had argued that they believed they had the right to use the sample due to their status as pioneers of the rap genre, and the fact that they had credited Spence as the original composer in the song.

Spence, who died in 2005, had also been a fan of the Beastie Boys, and had given his permission for the band to use the sample in question. However, his family argued that the band breached their agreement by commercializing the song without sharing the profits, and had made money off Spence's work without compensation.

The ruling also set a precedent for the future of sampling in the music industry. The court found that in order for a song to qualify as fair use under copyright laws, it must be significantly changed and must serve a new and transformative purpose. This means that simply using a sample from one work in a new piece is not enough to constitute fair use, and that original creators must be compensated for their work.

Overall, the ruling marks a significant victory for fair use and copyright law, and is a reminder that the creative process is a collaborative effort, with original creators entitled to recognition and compensation for their work.

Brazilian Coconut Beijinhos are a delicious and easy-to-make dessert that is perfect for any occasion. Here is a recipe for you to try:

Ingredients:
- 1 cup all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar, plus extra for rolling
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/2 cup melted butter
- 2 eggs
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 cup shredded coconut, plus extra for rolling
- 1/4 cup confectioners' sugar, for rolling

Instructions:
1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.
3. In a separate bowl, whisk together the melted butter, eggs, and vanilla extract. Set aside.
4. In a third bowl, combine the shredded coconut and confectioners' sugar. Set aside.
5. Roll the dough into 1-inch balls and then roll them in the coconut mixture. Place the balls on the prepared baking sheet.
6. Bake for 15-20 minutes, or until the cookies are golden brown.
7. Remove from the oven and let cool on a wire rack.
8. Roll the cooled cookies in the remaining coconut mixture.
9. Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days.

A Potts model-based community detection algorithm is employed to assess the hierarchical or multiresolution architecture of graphs with precision. This algorithm computes correlations between multiple versions (replicas) of the same graph across various resolutions. Notably, the identification of significant multiresolution structures is achieved through replicas displaying strong correlation. Quantitative estimates of optimal resolutions and structural strengths in graphs can be obtained via measures such as average normalized mutual information and variation of information. Since the method relies on comparative analysis, it can potentially be applied to any community detection model capable of evaluating multiple resolutions. Our approach differs from other models by avoiding the "resolution limit," resulting in superior accuracy. By using this model, the community detection algorithm demonstrates exceptional performance, enabling examination of graphs containing up to 40 million nodes and over 1 billion edges. Moreover, the multiresolution variant of the algorithm successfully solves systems consisting of at least 200,000 nodes and 10 million edges on a single processor with outstanding accuracy. The algorithm exhibits super-linear scaling, specifically O(L^{1.3}) for community detection and O(L^{1.3} log N) for its multiresolution counterpart, where L represents the number of edges and N denotes the number of nodes in the network.

Martino rebounded with four wins, including a first-round knockout of former world champion Maurice Blocker, before challenging for the IBF super welterweight title in 1994. He defeated champion Gianfranco Rosi by knockout in the eleventh round to win the title. He made one successful defense of the title before losing it to Rosi in a rematch in 1995.

Boyer's multifaceted book explains the genesis of religious concepts through the mind's cognitive inference systems, comparable to pareidolia and perceptions of religious imagery in natural phenomena resulting from face perception processes within the human brain. Boyer supports this naturalistic origin of religion with evidence from many specialized disciplines including biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, cognitive science, linguistics, evolutionary biology, cognitive psychology, evolutionary psychology, neuroscience, and information processing. Religion Explained frames religious practices and beliefs in terms of recent cognitive neuroscience research in the modularity of mind. This theory involves cognitive "modules" ("devices" or "subroutines") underlying inference systems and intuitions. For instance, Boyer suggests culturally-widespread beliefs in "supernatural agents" (e.g., gods, ancestors, spirits, and witches) result from agent detection: the intuitive modular process of assuming intervention by conscious agents, regardless of whether they are present. "When we see branches moving in a tree or when we hear an unexpected sound behind us, we immediately infer that some agent is the cause of this salient event. We can do that without any specific description of what the agent actually is." Boyer cites E. E. Evans-Pritchard's classic Zande story about a termite-infested roof collapsing. For the anthropologist, the house caved in because of the termites. For the Zande, it was quite clear that witchcraft was involved. However, the Zande were also aware that the termites were the proximate cause of the incident. But what they wanted to know was why it happened at that particular time, when particular people were gathered in the house. Within Boyer's hypothesis, religion is a "parasite" (or "spandrel") offshoot from cognitive modules, comparable to the way the reading process is parasitic upon language modules. As I have pointed out repeatedly the building of religious concepts requires mental systems and capacities that are there anyway, religious concepts or not. Religious morality uses moral intuitions, religious notions of supernatural agents recruit our intuitions about agency in general, and so on. This is why I said that religious concepts are parasitic upon other mental capacities. Our capacities to play music, paint pictures or even make sense of printed ink-patterns on a page are also parasitic in this sense. This means that we can explain how people play music, paint pictures and learn to read by examining how mental capacities are recruited by these activities. The same goes for religion. Because the concepts require all sorts of specific human capacities (an intuitive psychology, a tendency to attend to some counterintuitive concepts, as well as various social mind adaptations), we can explain religion by describing how these various capacities get recruited, how they contribute to the features of religion that we find in so many different cultures. We do not need to assume that there is a special way of functioning that occurs only when processing religious thoughts. Boyer admits his explanation of religion is not a quick, shoot-from-the-hip solution of the kind that many people, either religious or not, seem to favor. There cannot be a magic bullet to explain the existence and common features of religion, as the phenomenon is the result of aggregate relevance – that is, of successful activation of a whole variety of mental systems.

The mean systemic pressure, or mean circulatory filling pressure, refers to the average pressure within the circulatory system when there is no blood flow. In contrast, the mean circulatory filling pressure encompasses the combined pressures in both the circulatory and pulmonary systems under the same conditions. Studies have shown that the mean systemic pressure in animal models averages around 7 mm Hg. This value serves as an indicator of the circulatory system's capacity relative to its blood volume, with factors such as circulating blood quantity and vascular smooth muscle tone influencing this relationship. There are different methods for measuring mean systemic pressure, leading to varying nomenclature. One method involves clamping key vessels and the other uses brief periods of cardiac arrest to assess redistribution. Additionally, it can be estimated in living patients through controlled breathing patterns while they're on a ventilator. This measurement helps track how medications impact venous tone when blood volume remains stable, or monitors hemodynamic shifts during significant blood loss.

Information flow is the branch of security that studies the leakage of
information due to correlation between secrets and observables. Since in
general such correlation cannot be avoided completely, it is important to
quantify the leakage. The most followed approaches to defining appropriate
measures are those based on information theory. In particular, one of the most
successful approaches is the recently proposed $g$-leakage framework, which
encompasses most of the information-theoretic ones. A problem with $g$-leakage,
however, is that it is defined in terms of a minimization problem, which, in
the case of large systems, can be computationally rather heavy. In this paper
we study the case in which the channel associated to the system can be
decomposed into simpler channels, which typically happens when the observables
consist of multiple components. Our main contribution is the derivation of
bounds on the (multiplicative version of) $g$-leakage of the whole system in
terms of the $g$-leakages of its components. We also consider the particular
cases of min-entropy leakage and of parallel channels, generalizing and
systematizing results from the literature. We demonstrate the effectiveness of
our method and evaluate the precision of our bounds using examples.

This paper presents the experimental study revealing weaker performance of
the automatic iris recognition methods for cataract-affected eyes when compared
to healthy eyes. There is little research on the topic, mostly incorporating
scarce databases that are often deficient in images representing more than one
illness. We built our own database, acquiring 1288 eye images of 37 patients of
the Medical University of Warsaw. Those images represent several common ocular
diseases, such as cataract, along with less ordinary conditions, such as iris
pattern alterations derived from illness or eye trauma. Images were captured in
near-infrared light (used in biometrics) and for selected cases also in visible
light (used in ophthalmological diagnosis). Since cataract is a disorder that
is most populated by samples in the database, in this paper we focus solely on
this illness. To assess the extent of the performance deterioration we use
three iris recognition methodologies (commercial and academic solutions) to
calculate genuine match scores for healthy eyes and those influenced by
cataract. Results show a significant degradation in iris recognition
reliability manifesting by worsening the genuine scores in all three matchers
used in this study (12% of genuine score increase for an academic matcher, up
to 175% of genuine score increase obtained for an example commercial matcher).
This increase in genuine scores affected the final false non-match rate in two
matchers. To our best knowledge this is the only study of such kind that
employs more than one iris matcher, and analyzes the iris image segmentation as
a potential source of decreased reliability.

Detecting buildings from satellite multispectral images poses significant challenges due to accurately extracting building footprints from high-resolution images. This research presents a novel deep learning method that incorporates various enhancements throughout the entire process. The initial dataset undergoes 2-sigma percentile normalization before undergoing ensemble modeling, which involves training three separate models using OpenStreetMap data. To enhance data labeling, Binary Distance Transformation (BDT) is applied, and the U-Net architecture is modified with batch normalization wrappers. Our approach's components are analyzed in relation to its overall detection accuracy. Furthermore, the study compares the proposed solution against the top-performing entries from the SpaceNet 2 competition, utilizing multispectral images of four cities - Las Vegas, Paris, Shanghai, and Khartoum, highlighting the significance of the developed method for achieving improved building detection accuracy.

As an advocacy body, Food First critiques the policies pursued by institutions like the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, emphasizing the shortcomings of the Green Revolution. This movement, popularized in the 1970s, aimed to increase crop yields but ultimately led to high costs without significant productivity gains compared to traditional farming methods. In recent years, there has been a renewed emphasis on the Green Revolution, particularly through the use of genetically modified organisms and high-yielding crops. However, Food First argues that this approach will exacerbate existing global disparities, and has released reports highlighting the need for more localized, sustainable agricultural approaches to foster fair and effective development.

Meanwhile, warm up the milk, eggs, and limoncello to room temperature. Start by zesting both lemons to get about 1 1/2 tablespoons of zest and then juice one lemon to obtain roughly 1/4 cup of juice. Set the juice aside. Prepare the cake pan by buttering it, covering the bottom with parchment paper, and buttering the paper too - make sure the pan is at least 2 inches tall. A springform pan works well for this recipe. Mix the dry ingredients - flour, sugar, salt, baking powder, and baking soda - in a separate bowl. Use a stand mixer with a whisk attachment to combine the wet ingredients: lemon zest, juice, olive oil, limoncello, eggs, and milk. I just finished watching "The Butterfly Effect" and I'm still trying to process my thoughts about it. The film had an intriguing premise - a man discovers that he has the ability to travel back in time and change events from his past, but each time he does, the present changes in unexpected ways.

I have to say, the first half of the movie was really engaging. The main character, Evan Treborn, played by Ashton Kutcher, is a likable guy who you can't help but feel for as he tries to navigate his way through life with this strange power. The scenes where he goes back in time and alters events are well-executed and suspenseful, leaving you wondering what will happen next.

But as the movie progresses, things start to fall apart. The plot becomes increasingly convoluted and hard to follow, with too many characters and subplots that don't add anything meaningful to the story. The dialogue also gets cheesier and more predictable, which takes away from the overall impact of the film.

One thing that really bothered me was the lack of consistency in the rules of time travel. It seems like the writers made up their own rules as they went along, without thinking through the consequences or logic of them. For example, why can Evan only go back in time to moments when he was in the same location? And how come he can change some things but not others? These questions are never adequately answered, leaving the viewer feeling frustrated and confused.

Despite these flaws, I did appreciate the attempt at exploring deeper themes such as the butterfly effect itself, the concept of fate vs free will, and the idea that our choices have consequences that ripple out beyond our own lives. However, these ideas could have been executed much better with tighter writing and a clearer vision.

Overall, I would say that "The Butterfly Effect" starts off strong but ultimately falls flat due to its poor execution and inconsistencies. If you're a fan of sci-fi or time travel movies, you might find it worth watching, but otherwise, there are definitely better options out there.

This book focuses on an aspect of World War II that is largely ignored in many history books – the Nazi looting of Europe and Russia and the Allied recovery and repatriation of stolen art. Little known to the general public, Hitler diverted his attention from the prosecution of the war to the systematic theft of Europe’s great art. His dream was to build the world’s greatest collection – The Führermuseum – in his hometown of Linz, Austria. European museum officials took extraordinary measures to protect art from Hitler and the ensuing war. When U.S. forces prepared to enter Europe, they assembled a special force of largely American and British museum directors, curators, and art historians known as the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives program (MFAA) section, attached to the Allied armies. These “Monuments Men” attempted to minimize damage to European monuments and architecture, then track down stolen works of art. Their effort would become one of the greatest “treasure hunts” in history. In the end, Allied forces located more than 1,000 repositories in mines and castles across Europe, many of which were filled with art, sculpture, furniture, archives, and other cultural property stolen by the Nazis. Edsel points out that thousands of pieces are still missing, such as Raphael’s Portrait of a Young Man from the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków, Poland. Rescuing Da Vinci tells this story through brief text and more than 460 photographs, 60 of which are in color. This group of photographs has never been published in a single book, and many have not been seen in decades. Images such as Michelangelo’s David entombed in brick for protection or a Rembrandt Self Portrait sitting atop crates in a salt mine, capture the story better than words could describe.

Francis Ford Coppola's 'Apocalypse Now' stands out not only as a masterpiece of cinema but also as a landmark work in film history, having won the coveted Palme d'Or at Cannes and continuing to be celebrated as a defining moment in cinematic history. Adapted from Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness,' the film delves deeper into the human experience of war rather than focusing solely on the Vietnam conflict, offering a profound exploration of the darker aspects of human nature and its effects on individuals. At its core, 'Apocalypse Now' tells a timeless tale of universal struggle, probing the complexities of human duality – encompassing morality, primal instincts, and the choices we make in life.

With its straightforward premise, the film follows U.S. Army Captain Benjamin Willard, played by Martin Sheen, as he embarks on a perilous journey downriver into Cambodia to assassinate Colonel Kurtz, a renegade leader who has become a self-proclaimed deity among the local population, driven mad by the chaos of war. Despite its seemingly simple setup, the film offers far more depth, taking viewers on a journey into the heart of madness and the darkness of humanity. This film would lend itself to endless analysis, revealing numerous themes and interpretations. In my perspective, the river represents both a means to reach Kurtz and a metaphor for the downward spiral into madness, as the characters grapple with their own descent into darkness. Each stage of the journey along the river further emphasizes the dehumanizing effects of war, introducing a new form of evil to the characters. 

The first stop, Lieutenant Kilgore, illustrates how his troops have succumbed to their passion for war, losing touch with humanity in the process. This segment showcases how the initial excitement of combat gradually gives way to desensitization and the demonization of the enemy, ultimately leading to the development of a new kind of evil within them.
