Current semantic segmentation approaches often rely on the U-Net framework, which combines an encoder-decoder structure. However, this design faces challenges when modeling global multi-scale context: (1) Each skip connection, used to align encoder and decoder features, can be ineffective due to mismatched feature sets at different stages, potentially harming segmentation accuracy; (2) In some cases, removing these skip connections altogether leads to better performance on specific datasets. To address these issues, we propose UCTransNet, a novel framework that incorporates the channel perspective with an attention mechanism. This approach replaces traditional skip connections with the Channel Cross fusion module (CCT) and Channel-wise Cross-Attention (CCA). CCT enables multi-scale channel-level information exchange through a sub-module, while CCA guides this exchange towards decoder features, mitigating ambiguity. Our proposal effectively resolves semantic gaps, resulting in improved automatic medical image segmentation outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that UCTransNet outperforms state-of-the-art models across various datasets and architectures, including those using transformers or U-shape frameworks, as showcased in its GitHub repository (https://github.com/McGregorWwww/UCTransNet).

Serves 4 as leftovers

Ingredients (for 2 servings):

1 tbsp butter, softened

1 medium butternut squash, peeled, seeded, and diced

1 onion, diced

3 garlic cloves, finely diced

1 (14.25-ounce) can chopped tomatoes

½ cup water

½ cup milk

1 cup butternut squash puree (about 1/2 pound)

salt

1 teaspoon ground black pepper

1 cup dry white wine

2 cups chicken stock, or water

1 cup fresh baby arugula, washed and chopped, and torn leaves for garnish

½ cup chopped fresh dill

4 cups fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves, plus more for garnish

Directions:

1. Heat a 15-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add butter and sauté until it reaches a depth of 10 inches (about 3 minutes). Remove from the heat and set aside.

2. When the butter is gone, add the butternut squash and onion. Cook for 5 more minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, then add the diced tomatoes, then the water, milk, and stir vigorously until the sauce thickens, about 1 minute. Season with salt and pepper, to taste. Transfer the mixture to a food processor and pulse until it separates and starts to form a smooth puree. Transfer the puree to a large saucepan.

3. Bring to a boil. Add 2 cups of the stock (or water) and reduce heat for 2 minutes. Stir in the baby arug. Reduce the heat for 10 seconds, then add the wine and remaining stock. Lower heat to a simmer and cook until the wine has reduced by almost half and the soup is thick, about 25 minutes, stirring occasionally.

4. Stir in the parsley, drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle with a pinch of salt and pepper, and serve. Garnish with fresh dill and parsley leaves.

Image segmentation remains a prominent area of research in computer vision due to its critical role in image processing, leading to a constant need for more effective methods. As a fundamental concept, clustering has been widely applied across various scientific disciplines and engineering fields, with many studies focusing on its integration into image segmentation techniques. Despite the success of existing approaches, further enhancements are necessary. This paper presents a new clustering-based image segmentation approach, placing emphasis on color spaces and utilizing the Lab color model. A variant of the popular K-means algorithm is employed, which overcomes the limitations associated with choosing an optimal distance metric, opting instead for the cosine distance measure. Subsequent filtering of the segmented image using a Sobel operator enhances the results, followed by analysis with the marker-based watershed algorithm to produce the final segmented outcome. The Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) metrics serve as indicators of performance evaluation.

1/4 teaspoon fresh ground pepper
5 cups chopped spinach, wilted (see Tip)

1 cup ham steak, diced
1/2 cup jarred roasted red pepper, chopped

Preheat oven to 375 degrees F. Coat a 7-by-11-inch glass baking dish or a 2-quart casserole with cooking spray. Whisk eggs, egg whites and milk in a medium bowl. The first four British men to be released from Guantanamo Bay are expected to return to the UK within weeks.

The men - Shaker Aamer, Jamil El-Banna, Richard Belmar and Omar Deghayes - will fly to Britain on private jets, the BBC understands.

They are among nine British residents held at the US detention camp in Cuba.

The four men are due to be freed after being cleared of any involvement in terrorism by a US military review panel.

The BBC's Caroline Wyatt in Washington says it is not yet clear when the other five men will be released.

She says the four men due to be freed will fly to a military base in the United States before boarding private jets for Britain.

The Pentagon is expected to make a formal announcement later on Thursday.

The four men have been held at Guantanamo Bay since 2002.

Shaker Aamer, 39, from London, has already been cleared for release by the US authorities but remains in detention.

Jamil El-Banna, 45, from west London, was seized in Afghanistan where he had gone to help with relief efforts.

Mr Deghayes, 37, from Brighton, is originally from Libya. He went to Afghanistan to fight against the Soviet Union's occupation in the 1980s.

Richard Belmar, 24, from north London, is of Jamaican descent.

For this dish, gather the following ingredients: 
1 lb fresh green beans, trimmed 
1 small red bell pepper, sliced 
2 pieces of bok choy, cut into strips 
1-inch piece of fresh ginger 
A pinch of ground coriander 
About 1/3 of a palmful of seafood seasoning (or Old Bay for added flavor) 
A dash of freshly ground black pepper 
Four (6 oz) fish fillets (black bass or sea bass work well) 
1/2 cup hoisin sauce 
1/4 cup freshly squeezed orange juice 
Finely chopped scallions and cilantro 
Preheat your oven to 425°F. Prepare four large sheets of aluminum foil, approximately 18 inches square. Divide the foil among four separate sections, placing one sheet aside. Place a quarter of the green beans, bell peppers, and bok choy at the bottom of each remaining section, followed by three slices of ginger. Mix together the coriander, seafood seasoning, and black pepper in a small bowl, sprinkling it over the fish fillets on top. Drizzle the combined hoisin sauce and orange juice evenly over the fish, finishing with some chopped scallions and cilantro. Fold the longer sides of the foil over the fish, then roll the shorter ends to seal the packets tightly. Place the parcels side by side on a baking sheet and bake for 15 minutes or until the fish is cooked through, indicated by its opacity. Serve immediately after removing from the oven.

Andrew Litton, born on May 16, 1959, in New York City, is an American orchestral conductor. Litton attended The Fieldston School before studying piano with Nadia Reisenberg and conducting with Sixten Ehrling at the Juilliard School of Music, earning degrees in both fields. Additionally, he took guidance from Walter Weller at the Salzburg Mozarteum and Edoardo Müller in Milan, and was tutored by John DeMaio. As the youngest winner of the BBC International Conductors Competition in 1982, Litton held positions including Assistant Conductor at Teatro alla Scala and the National Symphony Orchestra in Washington D.C., working alongside Mstislav Rostropovich. He participated in the Affiliate Artists Exxon-Arts Endowment Conductors Program and was later recognized with Yale University's Sanford Medal in 2003. Litton began his career with the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra, serving as principal conductor from 1988 to 1994 and remaining as conductor laureate. Following twelve years as Music Director of the Dallas Symphony Orchestra from 1994 to 2006, he became Music Director Emeritus. Litton then spent fourteen seasons as Artistic Director of the Minnesota Orchestra's Sommerfest concerts from 2003 to 2017.

Residual amplitude modulation (RAM) has significant impacts on the performance of laser interferometers employing heterodyne sensing, particularly in gravitational wave detection systems. Here, we investigate how RAM affects a sophisticated laser interferometer designed for this purpose. By introducing unwanted offset distortions in the cavity length signals, RAM alters the operating point of the optical cavities through feedback control, thus affecting the sensing matrix and subsequently compromising the precision of the multiple-degree-of-freedom control system's noise cancellation method. Moreover, detuned optical cavities introduce an opto-mechanical spring effect, further altering the sensing matrix. Through computer simulations, we establish requirements for acceptable levels of RAM for the Advanced LIGO detectors, demonstrating that the expected RAM level does not impede the detector's sensitivity.

Inositol (1,4,5) trisphosphate 3-kinase is an enzyme responsible for transferring a phosphate group from adenosine triphosphate to 1D-myo-inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, resulting in the formation of inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate. As part of the phosphotransferase family, ITP3K specifically transfers its gamma-phosphate to the 3-position of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, yielding inositol tetrakisphosphate or Ins(1,3,4,5)P4. Highly selective for the 1,4,5-isomer, ITP3K exclusively targets the 3-hydroxyl position, generating IP4. Known for their specificity, these enzymes have various designations, including 1D-myo-inositol-trisphosphate 3-kinase, ITP3K, ITPK, IP3-kinase, IP3-3-kinase, and Ins(1,4,5)P3 3-kinase. They can arise from different human genes - ITPKA, ITPKB, and ITPKC, or from fruit fly genes IP3K1 and IP3K2, which are referred to as wavy mutants. Found exclusively in metazoans, ITP3K enzymes do not exist in yeast or plant genomes, where they are encoded by the LFE-2 gene.

Brazilian Coconut Beijinhos are a delicious and easy-to-make Brazilian dessert. They are made with just a few simple ingredients, including sweetened condensed milk, butter, and coconut. Here is a recipe for Brazilian Coconut Beijinhos:

Ingredients:

- 1 can (14 oz) sweetened condensed milk
- 1/2 cup (1 stick) butter, melted
- 2 cups coconut, finely shredded
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 2 eggs
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

Instructions:

1. Preheat oven to 350°F (180°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a large bowl, combine sweetened condensed milk, melted butter, coconut, baking powder, and salt. Stir in flour until well combined.
3. Add eggs and vanilla extract, and mix until well combined.
4. Roll dough into 1-inch balls and place on prepared baking sheet.
5. Bake for 20-25 minutes, or until lightly browned.
6. Let cool on wire rack for 5 minutes before serving.

Pork Chops with Apples and Pancetta Recipe

Ingredients:
- 4 pork chops, thick-cut
- Salt and pepper
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 8 ounces pancetta, diced
- 2 large apples, cored and sliced
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 teaspoon dried thyme
- 1/4 cup chicken broth
- 2 tablespoons butter

Instructions:

1. Preheat oven to 400°F.
2. Season the pork chops with salt and pepper on both sides.
3. Heat the olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat. Add the pork chops and cook for 3-4 minutes on each side until nicely browned. Remove the pork chops from the skillet and set aside.
4. Add the diced pancetta to the same skillet and cook over medium heat until crispy, about 5-7 minutes.
5. Add the sliced apples, minced garlic, and dried thyme to the skillet. Cook for 2-3 minutes until the apples start to soften.
6. Pour in the chicken broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.
7. Place the pork chops back into the skillet, spooning some of the apple and pancetta mixture on top of the pork chops.
8. Dot the top of the apples with butter and bake in the preheated oven for 20-25 minutes until the pork chops are fully cooked and the apples are tender.
9. Serve the pork chops with apples and pancetta hot, garnished with fresh thyme if desired. Enjoy!

To make these traditional Sri Lankan porcupine buns, start by combining 250 grams of bread flour, 6 grams of sugar, 1 teaspoon of olive oil, 130 millilitres of water, 5 grams of active dry yeast, and half a teaspoon of salt in a large mixing bowl. Sifting the flour beforehand will help incorporate air evenly. Mixing everything together takes about a minute, then pour in the olive oil and water and continue mixing until combined. Kneading the dough by hand for about 10 minutes will develop the gluten. Cover the dough and let it rest in a warm environment for roughly 30 minutes before punching it down. Divide the dough into 15 equal portions, shaping each one into a ball. Roll out each ball into a thin disk, approximately 2 1/2 inches in diameter and 1/4 inch thick.

To create the sweet coconut filling, combine 50 millilitres of coconut syrup or corn syrup, half a teaspoon of cinnamon powder, and half a teaspoon of sugar in a saucepan, bringing the mixture to a boil at around 100C degrees using a thermometer. Once the syrup has cooled slightly, stir in 100 grams of desiccated coconut. The mixture should now be smooth and ready to use.

Place a small spoonful of this coconut mixture onto the center of each disk, then roll the dough into a ball. Shape the bun into an oval shape and use scissors to cut off the top, creating a pointed tip resembling a porcupine's quills. Place each bun on a piece of parchment paper, then steam them over boiling water for 10 minutes. Remove the buns from the steamer and arrange them on a serving dish. You can customize the buns with eyes, a mouth, and whiskers made from food coloring and coconut husk. Serve the warm porcupine buns and enjoy. There was a man named Mr. Smiggs living in London; he was a gentleman with a kind heart, rarely showing displeasure. On Christmas Eve, he and his wife were cozy in bed when the idea struck him to purchase a goose. The next morning, as soon as sunrise, he jumped out of bed and dressed quickly, saying to his wife, "Don't worry, my dear, I've decided to buy you the finest goose in town." He went to the local market and bought the goose, paying only one shilling, which he believed to be a fair price. However, unbeknownst to him, a mischievous youth had snatched the goose from under his arm. Mr. Smiggs shouted, "Hey, thief! Give me back my goose!" But the young boy just laughed and insulted him. A police officer intervened, arrested the boy, and returned the goose to its rightful owner. The boy was punished by spending ten days in jail before being released. When Mr. Smiggs returned home, he exclaimed, "Rush, my dear, prepare the goose I purchased for just one shilling. You don't need to worry, it's an affordable treat." His wife reassured him, "Don't worry, Mr. Smiggs, one shilling is indeed a bargain, especially during Christmas time – and look, it's exquisite." Mr. Smiggs replied, "It's Christmas time, so let's forget about our worries. We have a delicious goose, so please cook it well. Whatever the fate of those less fortunate may be, let's enjoy our meal and savor every bite, even down to the last bone."

Shares in US phone company MCI have risen on speculation that it is in takeover talks.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Qwest has bid $6.3bn (£3.4bn) for MCI. Other firms have also expressed an interest in MCI, the second-largest US long-distance phone firm, and may now table rival bids, analysts said. Shares in MCI, which changed its name from Worldcom when it emerged from bankruptcy, were up 2.4% at $20.15. Press reports suggest that Qwest and MCI may reach an agreement as early as next week, although rival bids may muddy the waters. The largest US telephone company Verizon has previously held preliminary merger discussions with MCI, Reuters quoted sources as saying.
Consolidation in the US telecommunications industry has picked up in the past few months as companies look to cut costs and boost client bases. A merger between MCI and Qwest would be the fifth billion-dollar telecoms deal since October. Last week, SBC Communications agreed to buy its former parent and phone trailblazer AT&T for about $16bn. Competition has intensified and fixed-line phone providers such as MCI and AT&T have seen themselves overtaken by rivals. Buying MCI would give Qwest, a local phone service provider, access to MCI's global network and business-based subscribers. MCI also offers internet services.
MCI was renamed after it emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in April last year. It hit the headlines as Worldcom in 2002 after admitting it illegally booked expenses and inflated profits. The scandal was a key factor in a global slide in share prices and the reverberations are still being felt today. Shareholders lost about $180bn when the company collapsed, while 20,000 workers lost their jobs. Former Worldcom boss Bernie Ebbers is currently on trial, accused of overseeing an $11bn fraud.
